title: Acute chest pain in general practice: cardiovascular examination
desc: This station involves a brief, focused chest pain history and a full cardiovascular examination of a 60-year-old smoker with hypertension and high cholesterol who walks into a general practice with acute chest pain. The candidate then interprets his observations and 12-lead ECG, and outlines the immediate management in general practice, the ambulance transfer for reperfusion and the safety netting.
focus: Cardiovascular examination, then recognising and managing a STEMI in general practice
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement at a general practice clinic. Phillip, a 60-year-old accountant, has walked in from his office nearby with chest pain that started this morning. His record lists hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia. Your GP supervisor has asked you to assess him. A practice nurse is available to help, and the practice has a 12-lead ECG machine, an automated external defibrillator and an emergency drug kit.
tasks: Take a brief, focused history of Phillip's chest pain and perform a cardiovascular examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Phillip's observations and his 12-lead ECG. Give an ISBAR handover that includes your interpretation, then your most likely diagnosis and differentials, your management here in general practice and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Phillip, a 60-year-old accountant. You are uncomfortable, sweaty and anxious, and you keep rubbing the middle of your chest. You are trying to play it down because you have a lot of work on. Lie on the bed propped up at 45 degrees with your shirt off when asked. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "I've got this awful pressure in my chest. It's probably just indigestion, but my secretary made me come over."

History (give only when asked):

  • The pain: it started about 40 minutes ago while you were sitting at your desk. It started at about 9:25 this morning. It is in the middle of your chest, a heavy pressure "like someone sitting on me", spreading down your left arm and up into your jaw. It is 7 out of 10 and has been constant since it started. Breathing, moving and changing position make no difference. It is not sharp, tearing or ripping and it does not go through to your back. It did not come on all at once at full strength; it built up over a few minutes.
  • With the pain: you feel sweaty, a bit sick (you have not vomited) and a little short of breath. No palpitations. No fainting, but you feel slightly light-headed.
  • Before today: for about 3 weeks you have had a tightness in your chest walking up the stairs from the car park. It went away within a few minutes of stopping. You did not mention it to anyone. You have never had a heart attack, an angiogram or a stress test.
  • Other causes (only if asked): no recent cold or flu, no fever. No recent surgery, long trips or time in bed, no leg swelling, no coughing up blood. You get the odd bit of heartburn after a big curry, but this feels nothing like it. No injury to your chest.
  • Medical history: high blood pressure and high cholesterol for about 10 years. No diabetes as far as you know. No stroke, bleeding problems, stomach ulcers or recent operations or head injury.
  • Medicines: ramipril and atorvastatin, every day. No blood thinners. If asked about erectile dysfunction tablets such as Viagra or Cialis: "No, never." No over-the-counter medicines or supplements.
  • Allergies: none known. You have taken aspirin before for headaches without any problem.
  • Smoking and alcohol: a packet of 20 cigarettes a day for the last 30 years (if asked how many: "20 a day"). You have never tried to quit. About two beers a night, three or four nights a week.
  • Family history: your father had a heart attack at 72. No sudden deaths in the family.
  • Social: you live at home with your wife. You work in an accounting firm across the road and it is a busy time of year. You drive.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you think it is indigestion or stress from work. Underneath, you are frightened because this is how your father's heart attack started. You were hoping for something for heartburn so you can get back to the office.

How Phillip changes:

  • If the candidate asks the nurse for an ECG, the nurse says, "I'll record it now", and the examiner hands it over in Part 2.
  • If the candidate asks for observations, give the vital signs from the Exam findings. If the candidate starts to count the breathing rate or take a temperature themselves, the examiner stops them and gives the values.
  • If the candidate gives aspirin, chew it. If they give GTN spray, say the pain eases slightly for a minute, then comes back the same; you get a mild headache.
  • If the candidate is calm and explains what they are doing, settle a little. If they rush without explaining, become more anxious.

Exam findings (the examiner gives these when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General inspection: overweight man, pale and sweaty, anxious, in moderate discomfort, holding his chest. Not cachectic, no oedema. No features of Marfan syndrome.
  • Vital signs: heart rate 96 beats/min, regular. Blood pressure 150/90 mmHg (right arm). If the candidate asks for or measures the BP in the other arm: 146/88 mmHg left arm. Respiratory rate 20 breaths/min. SpO2 96% on room air. Temperature 36.7°C.
  • Hands: cool and clammy. Tar staining of the right index and middle fingers. Capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, peripheral cyanosis or tendon xanthomata.
  • Pulses: radial pulse 96, regular, normal volume and character. No radio-radial or radio-femoral delay. Femoral pulses equal.
  • Neck: carotid pulses normal in character, no bruits. JVP 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees.
  • Face, eyes and mouth: bilateral corneal arcus. No xanthelasma, no conjunctival pallor, pupils equal and reactive. No central cyanosis, fair dentition, normal palate. No malar flush.
  • Precordium: no scars, pacemaker, visible pulsations or chest deformity. Breathing slightly fast, no accessory muscle use. Apex beat in the 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line, not displaced, normal character. No heaves or thrills.
  • Auscultation: S1 and S2 heard and normal. No added sounds, murmurs or pericardial rub, including in the left lateral position and sitting forward in expiration.
  • Lungs: resonant, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or effusion.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. No hepatomegaly, splenomegaly or ascites. Abdominal aorta not palpably expansile, no bruits.
  • Lower limbs: no pitting oedema. Peripheral pulses present and equal. No calf swelling or tenderness, no Achilles tendon xanthomata, normal hair and colour. No clubbing of the toes.
  • Bedside glucose (if asked): 6.4 mmol/L.

check.x: Professionalism
Washes hands, introduces self (name and role), confirms Phillip's identity, explains the examination and gains consent.
Positions Phillip on the bed at 45 degrees and exposes him to the waist, maintaining his dignity.
Acknowledges his pain and anxiety, stays calm, uses plain language and keeps the history brief so assessment is not delayed.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Onset and timing: started at rest about 40 minutes ago, constant and still present.
Site, character and radiation: central heavy pressure spreading to the left arm and jaw.
Severity (7 out of 10), and whether breathing, movement or position change it.
Associated symptoms: sweating, nausea, breathlessness, palpitations, light-headedness or fainting.

check.x: Asks about features of the other causes of chest pain:

kids.x: Tearing or ripping pain going through to the back, or pain that is at full strength from the start (aortic dissection).
Recent surgery, immobility or travel, leg swelling or coughing up blood (pulmonary embolism).
Recent viral illness, or pain worse lying flat and better sitting forward (pericarditis); reflux symptoms.

check.x: Asks about previous episodes and cardiac history: three weeks of chest tightness on stairs that settles with rest, and no previous heart attack, angiogram or stress test.
Confirms cardiovascular risk factors: hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia, smoking quantified (about 30 pack-years), diabetes, family history of heart disease and alcohol.
Asks about medicines and contraindications to treatment:

kids.x: Allergies, including to aspirin (none).
Erectile dysfunction medicines (sildenafil, tadalafil) recently taken, which would rule out GTN.
Anticoagulants, bleeding, peptic ulcer, previous stroke, recent surgery or head injury.

check.x: Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is indigestion or work stress, is frightened because of his father's heart attack, and wants to get back to work.
Examination
Recognises possible acute coronary syndrome early and asks the nurse to record a 12-lead ECG before starting the precordial examination (guideline target: within 10 minutes of first medical contact).
General inspection: distress and pain, pallor and sweating, body habitus, oedema, cachexia, and syndromic features such as Marfan syndrome.
Vital signs:

kids.x: Heart rate, and specifically asks for or measures BP in both arms (150/90 and 146/88 mmHg, no significant difference).
Asks for the respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature (the examiner gives them; the candidate does not measure them).

check.x: Peripheral examination:

kids.x: Hands: clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, tar staining (present), Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, peripheral cyanosis, capillary refill, tendon xanthomata.
Pulses: radial rate, rhythm, volume and character; radio-radial and radio-femoral delay.
Neck: carotid pulse character and bruits, and JVP height.
Face, eyes and mouth: conjunctival pallor, corneal arcus (present), xanthelasma, pupils, central cyanosis, dentition, high-arched palate, malar flush.

check.x: Precordium:

kids.x: Inspects for scars, a pacemaker, visible pulsations, chest deformity and the breathing pattern.
Palpates for a pacemaker, the apex beat (5th intercostal space, midclavicular line), heaves at the left parasternal edge and thrills over each valve area.
Auscultates all four valve areas, comments on S1 and S2, added sounds, murmurs and a pericardial rub.

Uses manoeuvres: left lateral position for the mitral area, sitting forward in expiration for the aortic and pulmonary areas, aortic and mitral areas in expiration and pulmonary and tricuspid in inspiration.

check.x: States they would examine the following to complete the examination (stating it earns the mark):

kids.x: Lungs: percusses and auscultates, including the bases for crackles or effusion (heart failure).
Abdomen: liver and spleen, ascites, and palpation and auscultation of the abdominal aorta.
Lower limbs: pitting oedema, peripheral pulses, Achilles tendon xanthomata, hair loss, pallor and clubbing of the toes.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the observations: alert, systolic BP 144 to 150 mmHg and SpO2 95 to 96% on room air, but heart and breathing rates are rising with unchanged pain; not hypotensive or hypoxaemic, so GTN can be given and oxygen is not needed.
Identifies new ST elevation in V1 to V4 with reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF.
Reads the ECG systematically (rate, rhythm, axis, intervals) and compares with the ECG from 2 years ago, noting the changes are new.

States that this meets STEMI criteria (new ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads, at least 2 mm in V2 and V3 in a man over 40) and localises it to the anterior wall (left anterior descending artery).
Concludes acute anterior STEMI with ongoing pain well within 12 hours of onset, needing emergency reperfusion.

Justifies the diagnosis against the differentials: dissection less likely (pain not tearing, equal arm pressures, normal pulses, no aortic regurgitation murmur), pericarditis less likely (territorial elevation with reciprocal change, no PR depression or rub), and pulmonary embolism less likely (no risk factors, normal saturation).
Management
Recognises that a general practice cannot provide reperfusion and calls 000 for an emergency ambulance straight away; does not let Phillip drive or be driven by his wife.
Gives aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dissolved, after confirming no allergy or active bleeding.
Gives GTN sublingually (400 microgram spray or 300 to 600 microgram tablet) every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if systolic BP is above 90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor in the last 24 to 48 hours.
Gives oxygen only if hypoxaemic (SpO2 below 93%), titrated to SpO2 93 to 96%, and states it is not needed at 95 to 96% on room air.
Obtains IV access (if able, without delaying transfer) and avoids intramuscular injections in case of fibrinolysis.
For severe pain, titrates an IV opioid: morphine 2.5 to 5 mg IV every 5 to 10 minutes, or fentanyl as an alternative.

Keeps Phillip monitored until the ambulance arrives: stays with him, has the defibrillator (AED) at the bedside, repeats observations and the ECG, and is ready to start CPR and defibrillate if he arrests.

States the reperfusion plan: paramedics transmit the ECG and pre-notify the catheterisation laboratory; primary PCI if achievable within 90 minutes of first medical contact, otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes if there is no contraindication.
In the ISBAR recommendation, states that the new and old ECGs and a letter (medicines, allergies, time of onset, times of aspirin and GTN) will go with Phillip.

Answering Phillip, explains in plain words that the ECG shows a heart attack from a blocked artery and why he needs an ambulance rather than his wife's car (risk of a dangerous heart rhythm, direct transfer to the catheter lab), and offers to call his wife.
Safety netting
Tells Phillip, while waiting for the ambulance, to say straight away if the pain gets worse or he feels faint, breathless or his heart races, and reassures him he will not be left alone.
Gives future warning signs in plain words: chest pain or discomfort that is severe, getting worse or lasting 10 minutes means call 000, and never drive himself.
Arranges follow-up after discharge: names at least two of GP review with the discharge summary, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation support (Quitline 13 78 48).

part2.lead: Here are Phillip's observations from the practice nurse and his 12-lead ECG, recorded at 10:12.
part2.patient:
Phillip is still in pain and anxious. His questions are read out as the fourth question. If the candidate covers the first two during management, credit them there:

  • "Am I having a heart attack?"
  • "Can't my wife just drive me to the hospital? It's only ten minutes away and I don't want a fuss."
  • "What should I do while we wait for the ambulance?"
  • "If I get through this, what do I do if it happens again, and what happens after the hospital?"

Agree to the ambulance if the candidate explains clearly why it is needed. If they agree to your wife driving you, accept it.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse, on the bed at 45 degrees, on room air.
handover.model:
Read: on arrival HR 96 regular, BP 150/90 mmHg, RR 20, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 36.7°C, alert, pain 7/10. Fifteen minutes later HR has risen to 102, BP 144/88 mmHg, RR 22, SpO2 95%, and the pain is unchanged at 7/10.

For Phillip: he is alert, not hypotensive and not hypoxaemic, and has no signs of heart failure on examination (clear lungs, normal JVP). The rising heart rate and breathing rate with ongoing pain show the problem is continuing, not settling. There is no inpatient observation chart in the clinic, but on the repeat set the respiratory rate of 22 and heart rate of 102 have risen above normal. Nothing is severely deranged (no hypotension or hypoxaemia), but rising heart and breathing rates with unchanged ischaemic chest pain mean a doctor must act now.

What it changes: systolic BP well above 90 mmHg means GTN can be given. SpO2 of 95 to 96% means no oxygen is needed. Repeat observations every 5 to 10 minutes while waiting for the ambulance.

rows.note: Practice nurse on arrival: pale and sweaty
Repeat set: pain unchanged, still sweaty

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (10:12)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, recorded at 10:12 by the practice nurse during ongoing chest pain. Standard calibration (10 mm/mV, 25 mm/s).

  • Rate: 98 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus, regular.
  • Axis: +30°.
  • PR interval: 160 ms. No PR depression.
  • QRS: 96 ms. No bundle branch block.
  • QT: 340 ms, QTc 435 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments: convex (coved) ST elevation in V1 (1.5 mm), V2 (3 mm), V3 (3 mm) and V4 (2 mm). ST elevation of 0.5 mm in aVL. ST depression of 1 mm in II, III and aVF. ST segments isoelectric in I, aVR, V5 and V6.
  • T waves: tall, broad-based T waves in V2 to V4. No T wave inversion.
  • Other: no pathological Q waves. No left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage.
  • Comparison: ECG in the practice record from 2 years ago (routine hypertension review): sinus rhythm 74 beats/min, normal axis and intervals, no ST segment or T wave changes. All the ST and T wave changes above are new.
  • Conclusion: sinus rhythm with new ST elevation in V1 to V4 (and 0.5 mm in aVL) with reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF; changes are new compared with the ECG from 2 years ago.
handover.model:
Read: sinus rhythm at 98 beats/min, normal axis, normal PR, QRS and QTc. New convex ST elevation in V1 to V4 (3 mm in V2 and V3), with tall, broad hyperacute T waves in V2 to V4, slight (0.5 mm) ST elevation in aVL and reciprocal ST depression in II, III and aVF. No PR depression and no Q waves yet. All of this is new compared with the ECG from 2 years ago.

For Phillip: this meets STEMI criteria: new ST elevation in at least two contiguous leads, at least 2 mm in V2 and V3 in a man over 40 and at least 1 mm in the other leads. The territory is the anterior wall, supplied by the left anterior descending artery; the slight elevation in aVL with inferior reciprocal depression points to a proximal LAD occlusion, before the first diagonal branch. With central pressure pain spreading to the arm and jaw, sweating and three weeks of exertional angina, this is an acute anterior STEMI with ongoing ischaemia about 50 minutes after onset. Reciprocal change and territorial distribution argue against pericarditis.

What it changes: he needs emergency reperfusion. Call 000 now and give aspirin. The paramedics should transmit the ECG so the cardiac catheterisation laboratory can be activated. Do not wait for a troponin. He is at risk of ventricular fibrillation, so keep the defibrillator at the bedside.

ask: You are now phoning the cardiology registrar at the nearest hospital with a cardiac catheterisation laboratory. Please give an ISBAR handover of Phillip, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Phillip now, here in general practice.
Phillip asks you: "Am I having a heart attack? Can't my wife just drive me? What do I do while we wait, and if it happens again, and after hospital?" Please answer him.
expect:
• Identify: self, medical student calling on behalf of Dr [GP supervisor] at the GP clinic. Patient is Phillip, 60.
  • Situation: acute anterior STEMI. Central chest pain for about 50 minutes, ongoing at 7/10.
  • Background: HTN and high cholesterol on ramipril and atorvastatin, 30 pack-years, 3 weeks of exertional angina; no allergies, anticoagulants, PDE5 inhibitors or bleeding risk.
  • Assessment: Obs: HR 96 to 102, RR 20 to 22, BP 150/90 then 144/88, equal arm pressures, SpO2 96 to 95% on room air. Not hypotensive or hypoxaemic, but tachycardia is developing and pain is unchanged. No murmur, clear lungs, normal JVP. ECG: sinus rhythm 98, normal axis, PR, QRS and QTc. New convex ST elevation V1 to V4 (3 mm in V2 and V3), which meets STEMI criteria, slight elevation in aVL, reciprocal depression in II, III and aVF, hyperacute T waves. Anterior territory, proximal LAD. All new compared with the ECG from 2 years ago.
  • Recommendation: 000 called; aspirin 300 mg being given; please accept for primary PCI / advise on cath lab activation. New and old ECGs and a letter (medicines, allergies, onset time, drug times) will go with him.

Most likely: acute anterior STEMI. For it: central pressure pain at rest spreading to the left arm and jaw, sweating, nausea, three weeks of new-onset exertional angina, multiple risk factors, and new ST elevation in V1 to V4 with reciprocal change.

  • Acute aortic dissection (must exclude): hypertensive smoker. Against: pain not tearing or going to the back, equal arm pressures, no radio-femoral delay, no aortic regurgitation murmur.
  • Acute pericarditis: against: territorial ST elevation with reciprocal depression, no PR depression, pain not positional or pleuritic, no rub, no viral illness.
  • Pulmonary embolism: against: no risk factors, SpO2 96%, normal calves, pain not pleuritic.
  • Reflux or oesophageal spasm: his own idea. Against: radiation, sweating and the ECG.

1. Call 000 now for an emergency ambulance. A GP clinic cannot do reperfusion. He must not drive or be driven.
  2. Aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed (no allergy, no bleeding).
  3. GTN sublingually (400 microgram spray or 300 to 600 microgram tablet) every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if systolic BP above 90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor in the last 24 to 48 hours.
  4. Oxygen only if hypoxaemic (SpO2 below 93%), titrated to 93 to 96%. None needed at 95 to 96%.
  5. IV access if able, without delaying transfer; no IM injections (possible fibrinolysis).
  6. Severe pain: morphine 2.5 to 5 mg IV titrated, or fentanyl as an alternative.
  7. Monitor: stay with him, AED at the bedside, repeat observations and ECG.
  8. Reperfusion: paramedics transmit the ECG. Primary PCI if achievable within 90 minutes of first medical contact, otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes.

• Plain words: yes, a heart attack from a blocked heart artery.
  • The car: no; he could have a dangerous heart rhythm on the way, and the ambulance has a defibrillator and goes straight to the cath lab; offer to call his wife.
  • While waiting: tell me at once if the pain worsens or he feels faint, breathless or his heart races; he will not be left alone.
  • In future: call 000 if pain is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes, and never drive himself.
  • After hospital: GP review with the discharge summary, cardiac rehabilitation, Quitline 13 78 48.

ddx.for: Central pressure pain at rest spreading to the left arm and jaw with sweating and nausea, three weeks of exertional chest tightness, smoker with hypertension and high cholesterol, and new ST elevation in V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior depression.
A 60-year-old hypertensive smoker with severe acute chest pain.
ddx.against: Pain built up over minutes, is not tearing and does not go to the back, arm pressures are equal (150/90 and 146/88 mmHg), there is no radio-femoral delay and no aortic regurgitation murmur.
ST elevation is territorial with reciprocal depression and no PR depression, the pain is not pleuritic or positional, there is no rub and no recent viral illness.

ddx.for: Chest pain with mild breathlessness and a rising heart rate.
ddx.against: No surgery, immobility, travel, leg swelling or haemoptysis, SpO2 96% on room air, normal calves and non-pleuritic pain.

ddx.for: He thinks it is indigestion, has occasional heartburn and is nauseated.
ddx.against: He says it feels nothing like his heartburn, and the radiation to the arm and jaw, the sweating and the ECG point to the heart.

guide:
Run Part 1 as a combined station. A brief history (about 3 minutes) is expected, then the cardiovascular examination. Prompt "please move on to the examination" at about 4 minutes if the history is still running. Give the findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate starts to count the breathing rate or take a temperature, stop them and give the values. Credit the ECG request (item 13) only if it is made before the candidate starts the precordial examination (ideally within the first 2 to 3 minutes); a request made after the examination is complete does not earn item 13. Credit aspirin, GTN or calling for help given in Part 1 against the matching Part 2 items. Give the left-arm BP only if the candidate asks for both arms. In Part 2, hand over both results together and ask all four questions in order. Phillip's questions are the fourth question (the first two may also come up during management, and are credited wherever they are answered); his questions earn the plain-language explanation and the three safety-netting items (what to report while waiting, future warning signs and 000, follow-up after discharge).

A high-performing candidate asks for an ECG within the first minutes, takes a tight pain history that includes dissection features and contraindications to aspirin, GTN and fibrinolysis, and examines fluently, including both arm pressures and radio-femoral delay. They read the ECG systematically, name the anterior STEMI and the criteria, call 000 first, and give aspirin 300 mg, GTN with the BP and PDE5 checks, oxygen only if hypoxaemic, IV access without delaying transfer and titrated opioid. They keep the defibrillator at the bedside, state the reperfusion time targets and firmly but kindly refuse the wife's car.

A borderline candidate performs a complete but slow examination without asking for an ECG, misses the reciprocal changes or the comparison with the old ECG, gives routine oxygen, or plans to phone the hospital or wait for a troponin instead of calling 000. The source case requires recognising the setting and calling 000 for full marks on management. A candidate who lets Phillip be driven to hospital is unsafe.
explain:
The diagnosis: acute anterior STEMI

Phillip has central pressure pain at rest spreading to the left arm and jaw, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. It was preceded by three weeks of new exertional angina, in a 60-year-old with hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia and a 30 pack-year smoking history. His ECG shows new ST elevation in V1 to V4 with hyperacute T waves, slight ST elevation in aVL and reciprocal depression in the inferior leads. All of this is new compared with his ECG from 2 years ago. That is an acute anterior STEMI from occlusion of the proximal left anterior descending artery. Anyone presenting with possible acute coronary syndrome should have a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact. In a real consultation the ECG comes before a complete examination.

Reading the ECG

  • STEMI criteria: new ST elevation at the J point in at least two contiguous leads, at least 2 mm in V2 and V3 in men aged 40 or over (1.5 mm in women) and at least 1 mm in the other leads. Left bundle branch block (new or old) with ongoing ischaemic symptoms is treated as a STEMI equivalent.
  • Territory: V1 to V4 is anterior (LAD). II, III and aVF is inferior (usually the right coronary artery). I, aVL, V5 and V6 is lateral (circumflex or diagonal).
  • Supporting features: reciprocal depression and hyperacute T waves support infarction. In anterior STEMI, ST elevation in aVL with inferior ST depression suggests a proximal LAD occlusion, before the first diagonal branch. Widespread concave elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change suggests pericarditis.
  • Do not delay transfer for a troponin. The ECG and history are enough to act on.

Differentials that matter

  • Aortic dissection must be considered before antithrombotic treatment. Look for tearing pain to the back, maximal at onset, a difference of more than 20 mmHg between the arms, pulse deficits, radio-femoral delay or an aortic regurgitation murmur. Phillip has none of these.
  • Pericarditis: pleuritic, positional pain, a rub and diffuse ST changes.
  • Pulmonary embolism: risk factors, pleuritic pain, hypoxaemia, tachycardia.
  • Reflux or oesophageal spasm: a diagnosis of exclusion when the ECG is abnormal.

Management in general practice

The key step is recognising that a general practice cannot provide reperfusion: call 000. Never send the patient by private car, because ventricular fibrillation is most likely in the first hours. While waiting:

  • Aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dissolved, unless he is allergic or actively bleeding.
  • GTN sublingually (400 micrograms, 1 spray, every 5 minutes up to 3 doses) if systolic BP is above 90 mmHg. Avoid it after a PDE5 inhibitor (24 hours for sildenafil or vardenafil, 48 hours for tadalafil) and be cautious in right ventricular infarction.
  • Oxygen only if hypoxaemic (SpO2 below 93%), titrated to SpO2 93 to 96%. The Heart Foundation guideline does not recommend routine oxygen in patients who are not hypoxaemic.
  • IV access if able, without delaying transfer. Avoid intramuscular injections in case fibrinolysis is given.
  • Titrated IV opioid for severe pain: morphine 2.5 to 5 mg every 5 to 10 minutes, or fentanyl 25 to 50 micrograms every 5 to 10 minutes.
  • Monitoring: stay with the patient with a defibrillator at the bedside, and repeat the ECG and observations.

Reperfusion follows the Heart Foundation/CSANZ guideline for STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset. Primary PCI is preferred if it can be delivered within 90 minutes of first medical contact. Otherwise fibrinolysis is given within 30 minutes if there is no contraindication, often by paramedics before hospital in regional areas. This is why asking about bleeding, stroke, recent surgery and anticoagulants matters. Paramedics transmit the ECG so the catheterisation laboratory can be activated. Further antiplatelet and anticoagulant treatment is decided by the receiving cardiology team.

The cardiovascular examination (source teaching)

Position the patient at 45 degrees, exposed to the waist. Look for distress, cachexia and syndromic features such as Marfan syndrome (or Turner syndrome in a female patient).

  • Hands: clubbing (endocarditis, cyanotic heart disease), splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes and Janeway lesions (endocarditis), tar staining (smoking), cyanosis, capillary refill and tendon xanthomata (familial hypercholesterolaemia).
  • Pulses: radio-radial delay suggests subclavian stenosis or dissection. Radio-femoral delay suggests coarctation.
  • Neck: carotid character and bruits, and the JVP.
  • Face: corneal arcus and xanthelasma (lipids), Argyll Robertson pupils (syphilitic aortitis), central cyanosis, dental decay (endocarditis source), a high-arched palate (Marfan) and malar flush (mitral stenosis).
  • Precordium: inspect, palpate the apex, heaves and thrills, then auscultate each area with manoeuvres. Left lateral brings out the mitral area; sitting forward in expiration brings out aortic regurgitation; left-sided sounds are louder in expiration and right-sided sounds in inspiration.
  • Completion: lung bases, liver, aorta and ascites, and the lower limbs for oedema, pulses and xanthomata.

In ACS the examination is often normal. Its job is to find complications (heart failure, a new mitral regurgitation murmur, shock) and to exclude dissection.

Safety netting and follow-up

While waiting, Phillip should report any worsening straight away and should not be left alone. Afterwards, the Heart Foundation warning signs action plan applies: if chest discomfort is severe, getting worse or lasts 10 minutes, call 000 and do not drive. After discharge, the ACSQHC Acute Coronary Syndromes Clinical Care Standard expects:

  • early GP review with the discharge summary
  • referral to cardiac rehabilitation
  • secondary prevention medicines
  • smoking cessation support.
points: Chest pain that may be cardiac needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact, before a complete examination.

STEMI is new ST elevation in two or more contiguous leads (at least 2 mm in V2 and V3 in men 40 or over, 1 mm elsewhere); V1 to V4 is the anterior wall (LAD), and reciprocal change supports infarction over pericarditis.
In general practice, call 000: never send a STEMI patient by private car, and do not wait for a troponin.

While waiting: aspirin 300 mg, GTN 400 micrograms sublingually every 5 minutes up to 3 doses if systolic BP is above 90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor, oxygen only if hypoxaemic (SpO2 below 93%), IV access without delaying transfer and no IM injections, titrated IV opioid, and a defibrillator at the bedside.
Primary PCI is preferred if achievable within 90 minutes of first medical contact; otherwise fibrinolysis within 30 minutes if not contraindicated.
Check both arm pressures, pulses and for an aortic regurgitation murmur to look for aortic dissection before antithrombotic treatment.
